objectives: Compare modes + mode share — auto, transit, cycling, walking, micromobility.
Apply transit planning — BRT, LRT, heavy + commuter rail, frequency vs coverage.
Synthesize cycling + pedestrian + Vision Zero + 15-minute city.

slides.title: Modes + mode share: auto, transit, cycling, walking, micromobility — and induced demand
slides.body:
**Urban transportation** moves people + goods within and between cities. The mode mix (the *mode share* — fraction of trips by each mode) defines a city's spatial form, climate footprint, equity profile, and street life.

**Mode-share archetypes** (urban commuting, recent data):
- **U.S. average**: ~76% private auto (solo + carpool), ~5% transit, ~3% walk + bike + other, ~16% work from home (rising post-2020).
- **NYC** (city only): ~32% transit, ~28% auto, ~10% walk, very high WFH. Outer-borough numbers more auto-heavy.
- **Tokyo (23 wards)**: ~58% rail, ~25% bike + walk, ~10% auto, ~7% bus.
- **Copenhagen**: ~28% bike, ~26% walk + transit, ~32% auto (CBD).
- **Amsterdam**: similar bike + walk dominance.
- **Bogotá**: ~30% transit (TransMilenio + Sitp), ~9% bike, large walk share.
- **Curitiba**: ~45% BRT-driven transit.

**Mode choice** depends on: trip purpose + length, time-of-day, weather, household income, vehicle availability, urban form (density, mix, design), transit quality, parking cost + availability, congestion. Disaggregate logit models (McFadden's discrete-choice models, Nobel 2000) underpin travel-demand forecasting.

**Induced demand + the Downs-Thomson paradox**:
- **Anthony Downs (1962, 'The Law of Peak-Hour Expressway Congestion'; *Stuck in Traffic* 1992) + John Thomson**: in a congested network with substitute transit, adding road capacity attracts more drivers until congestion returns to equilibrium. The new auto equilibrium is *worse* if the substitution drains transit ridership, raising transit fares + lowering frequency.
- **Empirical confirmation**: Duranton + Turner (2011 *AER*, 'The Fundamental Law of Road Congestion') — using IV with planned-highway data — find a near-unitary elasticity of VMT with respect to road capacity. *Building more roads does not reduce congestion*.
- **Implication**: the only ways to reduce congestion are demand-side — pricing (next), better substitutes (transit), or different urban form (density + mix reduce trip lengths).

**The Braess paradox**:
- **Dietrich Braess (1968, *Unternehmensforschung*)**: in some network configurations, adding a new edge *increases* total travel time at equilibrium because selfish routing reroutes more flow through the bottleneck. Counter-examples exist in real networks: closing Cheonggyecheon expressway in Seoul (2003) + 42nd Street in NYC (1990 Earth Day) improved overall flow.
- A reminder that traffic-engineering intuition is unreliable; networks have emergent + non-monotone behavior.

**Congestion pricing (Vickrey)**:
- **William Vickrey (Nobel 1996, sadly posthumous by 3 days)** advocated marginal-cost congestion pricing from the 1950s. The idea: charge each driver the externality they impose on others (delay + emissions + crash risk). Toll varies with time of day + corridor demand.
- **Real implementations**: Singapore Area Licensing Scheme (1975) → Electronic Road Pricing (1998); London Congestion Charge (2003, Ken Livingstone); Stockholm (2006 trial → permanent); Milan (2008); New York City (Manhattan CBD pricing 2025-, after years of delay). Evidence: ~20-30% reduction in cordon-entry traffic; improved bus speeds + reduced emissions + sustained over years.
- Politically hard. Equity concerns (regressive on low-income drivers) addressed via revenue recycling (transit investment, low-income credits).

**Micromobility** (mid-2010s-): dockless e-scooters (Bird, Lime), e-bikes, bike-share (Citi Bike, Vélib', Bicing), mopeds. Short trips, last-mile + first-mile, complement transit. Regulatory + safety issues + clutter; cities now permit + cap fleets.

slides.title: Transit planning: BRT, LRT, heavy + commuter rail, Curitiba, TransMilenio, Walker's frequency vs coverage
slides.body:
**Public transit** is the mode that determines whether a city can have urban form denser than ~10000/mi² without congestion meltdown. Modes vary in capacity, cost, speed, and use case.

**Mode capacities** (passengers per hour per direction, PPHPD):
- **Mixed-traffic bus**: ~1500 PPHPD.
- **Bus Rapid Transit (BRT)**: ~5000-25000 PPHPD (depending on dedicated infrastructure).
- **Light rail (LRT)**: ~10000-20000 PPHPD.
- **Heavy rail metro**: ~30000-80000+ PPHPD (Shanghai Line 9 + NYC L + Hong Kong MTR push the upper bound).
- **Commuter rail**: ~10000-40000 PPHPD; longer headways, longer trips.
- **Cars (freeway lane)**: ~2000-2400 PPHPD.

The order-of-magnitude advantage of rail over auto is the structural reason dense cities (NYC, Tokyo, Paris, London, Shanghai) require metros — there is no other technology that moves so many people through so little space.

**Bus Rapid Transit (BRT)**:
- Dedicated lanes + station platforms + prepaid boarding + signal priority — bus operations approaching rail performance at a fraction of capital cost.
- **Curitiba, Brazil**: Jaime Lerner (architect, 3-term mayor, 1971-1992). The original BRT system + the most influential. Trinary road + transit-oriented land use co-designed. *Network of Direct Lines* + *Speedy Bus*.
- **Bogotá TransMilenio (2000-)**: largest BRT in the world; ~2.5M daily riders peak; 113 stations + 142 km dedicated. Enrique Peñalosa's mayoral signature; ITDP gold-standard.
- **Guangzhou BRT (2010)**: highest-capacity BRT in the world (~27000 PPHPD).
- **Other**: Quito, Mexico City Metrobús, Jakarta TransJakarta, Lagos, Dar es Salaam DART, Cleveland HealthLine.

**Light rail (LRT)**: dedicated track at-grade or elevated; medium capacity; lower cost than heavy rail; Portland MAX, Calgary CTrain, Houston Light Rail, Manchester Metrolink, Strasbourg, Bordeaux.

**Heavy rail metro**: grade-separated; highest capacity; required for highest densities. Tokyo (Yamanote + 13 metro lines + ~40M daily riders system-wide), Beijing (largest by ridership), Shanghai (largest by track-km), Moscow, Seoul, NYC (oldest U.S. system 1904), London (1863 first), Paris (1900), Madrid, Mexico City.

**Commuter rail / regional rail**: longer-distance + lower-frequency than metro; suburbs to CBD. NYC LIRR + Metro-North + NJ Transit; Boston MBTA Commuter Rail; London + Paris RER; Tokyo Yamanote + JR East lines; Munich S-Bahn; Stockholm Pendeltåg.

**High-speed rail (HSR)**: 250+ km/h dedicated track for intercity. Japan Shinkansen (1964 first, ~9000 km network); France TGV (1981-); Spain AVE; China (~45000 km, largest network); South Korea KTX; Italy Frecciarossa. U.S.: Acela (Boston-DC, ~240 km/h max but averages lower); California HSR under construction; Texas HSR proposed.

**Frequency vs coverage — Jarrett Walker, *Human Transit* (2012)**:
- **Walker (transit consultant + public-policy writer)**: every transit-network design is a trade-off on the *frequency-coverage spectrum*. **High-frequency** networks concentrate service on the densest corridors → most-effective per ride but skip low-density areas. **High-coverage** networks spread service thin → reach everyone but each route is infrequent + slow + has low ridership.
- *Human Transit* argues the choice is *political* (what does the city value?), not technical. Houston Reimagined (2015) + Auckland (2016) + Brisbane redesigns all explicitly chose high-frequency + accepted lower coverage.
- **Transit ridership drivers**: density + mix near stations, walkability of station areas, service frequency (the *15-min frequency threshold* — service waitable without a schedule), reliability, fares.

**Fare policy + integration**:
- Distance-based (Tokyo, Shanghai) vs flat (NYC subway) vs zone (London).
- Integrated multi-modal fares (Stockholm SL, London Oyster, Singapore EZ-Link).
- Income-based reduced fares + free youth fares (Boston, Kansas City fare-free).
- Mobility-as-a-Service (MaaS) integration platforms (Helsinki Whim).

**Transit-oriented development (TOD)** (lesson 1 + Calthorpe): co-locating density + mix + walkability with high-quality transit. The bidirectional condition for rail-supported urbanism.

slides.title: Bicycle + pedestrian + Vision Zero + complete streets + the 15-minute city (Moreno)
slides.body:
**Walking + cycling** are the cheapest, healthiest, lowest-emission, lowest-footprint modes. They were the default of pre-automotive cities + are central to every contemporary planning movement (New Urbanism, smart growth, TOD, sustainable + 15-minute city).

**Copenhagen — the bicycle exemplar**:
- Bike mode share for commuting: ~49% in central Copenhagen; ~28% city-wide.
- ~390 km of bike lanes + ~12k bike parking spaces at Nørreport Station.
- *Copenhagenize Index* ranks bike-friendly cities globally; Copenhagen + Utrecht + Amsterdam + Antwerp consistently top.
- Built on decades of design: cycle tracks (protected lanes physically separated from cars + sidewalks); intersection-priority signals; integrated transit transfer.
- Cost: extensive but a fraction of equivalent road capacity. ROI from health + congestion + emissions reduction.

**Dutch infrastructure**: the Netherlands invented + perfected the *fietsstraat* (bike street), the *roundabout-for-bikes*, the protected intersection. ~27% national bike mode share; in Houten + Groningen + Utrecht over 40%. The 1970s *Stop de Kindermoord* (Stop the Child Murder) movement responded to high traffic-deaths of children + drove a national investment in cycling infrastructure.

**Protected bike lanes / cycle tracks**: physically separated from motor traffic (curb, bollard, planter, parked-car buffer). Critical for safety perception + mode-share growth. NYC, Vancouver, Montreal (over 1000 km of bike network), Seville (built ~100 km in 3 years, raising bike share 1% → 7%), Bogotá (Ciclorrutas + Sunday Ciclovía).

**Vision Zero — Sweden + the global movement**:
- **Vision Zero** originated in Sweden's 1997 traffic-safety legislation: *no fatal or serious injury in the transport system is acceptable*.
- Premise: humans make mistakes; the system must be designed so mistakes do not produce death. Speed management, separation of users, predictable design.
- Sweden's road-deaths-per-capita are ~⅓ the U.S. rate.
- **U.S. adoption**: NYC 2014 (first major U.S. city; Mayor de Blasio + DOT Commissioner Polly Trottenberg); Seattle, San Francisco, Boston, Portland, Washington DC, Los Angeles + ~50 U.S. cities.
- Tools: lower speed limits (20 mph residential, 25 arterial); road diets; protected lanes; daylighting at intersections; leading pedestrian intervals; automated enforcement.
- Evidence: NYC pedestrian deaths down ~40% (2014-22); broader U.S. trends mixed — increased SUV + truck sizes + driver smartphone use + COVID-era driving have worked against Vision Zero efforts.

**Complete Streets**: U.S. policy framework (Smart Growth America + NCSC) — design streets for all users (pedestrians, cyclists, transit, motorists, freight) of all ages + abilities. ~1500 U.S. jurisdictions have Complete Streets policies. Counter to the postwar default of designing for through-auto-traffic.

**Vision Zero + Complete Streets converge on**: lower speed limits, road diets (reducing travel lanes), protected bike + bus + pedestrian infrastructure, accessible (ADA) crossings, daylighting + curb extensions, reducing curb radii at intersections.

**Carlos Moreno — the 15-minute city (2016-)**:
- **Moreno** (Sorbonne, Franco-Colombian urbanist; *Droit de cité* 2020): every resident should reach daily needs (work, school, food, health, leisure, culture) within a 15-minute walk or bike ride from home.
- Six functions × four conditions (proximity, diversity, density, ubiquity).
- **Paris under Anne Hidalgo (mayor 2014-)** is the flagship: pedestrianized Seine quays, *coronapistes* (pop-up COVID bike lanes made permanent), school streets, Rue de Rivoli car-free.
- *Adopted globally*: Melbourne (*20-minute neighbourhood*), Portland (*20-minute neighborhoods*), Barcelona superblocks (lesson 6), Milan, Bogotá, Buenos Aires, Ottawa.
- *Critiques + conspiracies*: ill-founded conspiracy theories framed 15-min cities as climate-lockdown plots (2023-); Moreno + cities have pushed back. The actual proposal is simple urban-form + accessibility.

**Tactical urbanism**: low-cost, quick-build interventions — paint-and-post bike lanes, parking-day parklets, pedestrian plazas (NYC Times Square 2009), open streets (Sunday Ciclovía Bogotá 1974-; replicated worldwide). A way to demonstrate change + build constituency before permanent redesign.

**Synthesis — what makes a transportation-equity-and-climate-coherent city**:
1. High-frequency transit network (Walker).
2. Dense + mixed land use near stations (Calthorpe TOD).
3. Walkable + cyclable + protected infrastructure (Dutch + Danish models).
4. Congestion + parking pricing (Vickrey + Shoup).
5. Vision Zero design + speed management.
6. 15-minute-city accessibility planning.
7. Equity (transit + bike access in underserved neighborhoods).

Lesson 7 returns to the equity + environmental-justice dimensions. Lesson 6 picks up the infrastructure side.

question.question: Apply Downs-Thomson + induced demand to a road-widening proposal
question.goal: A metro's main commute corridor is widened from 4 to 6 lanes. Predict the effects + propose a better policy.

steps.prompt: What does the immediate (week-1) flow look like?

acceptedAnswers: more capacity, faster trips, congestion temporarily relieved

steps.reveal: Week-1: the wider road has more capacity at given demand; speeds rise + congestion drops. This is the political pitch for widening — visible short-run relief.

steps.prompt: What does Downs-Thomson predict over 1-3 years?

acceptedAnswers: lower travel times attract new auto trips (latent demand, mode switch from transit, land-use change), and congestion returns to roughly the prior equilibrium

hints: Latent demand + mode switch + land use react.
steps.reveal: Lower travel times unleash latent demand (trips previously suppressed), pull commuters from transit + carpool to solo driving, and encourage development further from CBD (induced sprawl). Within 1-3 years, congestion returns to roughly the prior equilibrium. Duranton + Turner (2011 AER) find a near-unitary elasticity of VMT to road capacity — the *Fundamental Law of Road Congestion*.

steps.prompt: What's the joint Downs-Thomson effect on transit?
steps.motivation: The paradox is jointly with substitutes.

acceptedAnswers: transit ridership falls; fare revenue falls; service is cut or fares raised; quality declines and the new auto equilibrium is worse than the old one

hints: Mode substitution drains the transit network.
steps.reveal: Downs-Thomson: with shared origin-destination pairs, mode share is set so that car + transit generalized cost is equal at the margin. Improving driving draws ridership away from transit; transit fixed costs spread over fewer riders → higher unit cost → cuts in service / higher fares → further loss of ridership. The equilibrium can be strictly worse than the original.

steps.prompt: What policy package is supported by the evidence instead of widening?

acceptedAnswers: congestion pricing (vickrey), invest in transit + bike + ped + tod, eliminate parking minimums (shoup), upzone near transit — addressing demand and improving substitutes rather than expanding auto supply

steps.reveal: The supply-of-roads channel is the wrong lever. Effective alternatives: (1) Congestion pricing — Vickrey + London + Singapore + NYC 2025 — to price the externality; (2) Invest in transit + bike + pedestrian infrastructure to expand substitutes; (3) Shoup-style parking-price + minimum reform; (4) Calthorpe TOD + upzoning near transit (lesson 2) to reduce trip lengths + auto-dependence. Combined demand + substitute + land-use changes are the only durable solution to congestion.

question.question: Why is Vision Zero (Sweden 1997-) considered a paradigm shift in traffic-safety policy?
options: Vision Zero (Sweden 1997 traffic-safety legislation) reframes road deaths from *acceptable cost of mobility* to *unacceptable system failure*. The premise: humans make mistakes; the system must be designed so mistakes do not produce death — by managing speeds, separating users, and using predictable design. This inverts traditional traffic engineering's focus on *driver education* + *enforcement* + *minimum standards*. Sweden's road-deaths-per-capita are ~⅓ the U.S. rate. NYC adopted Vision Zero in 2014 + has cut pedestrian deaths ~40% through 2022; ~50 other U.S. cities have followed. Tools include lower speed limits, road diets, protected lanes, daylighting, leading pedestrian intervals, automated enforcement. Vision Zero + Complete Streets + the 15-minute city (Moreno) together define the contemporary safe + walkable urbanism agenda.

question.question: Designing a corridor redesign
question.prompt: A 4-lane urban arterial (~20000 ADT, ~35 mph posted, residential + light commercial frontage, 9 pedestrian deaths in past 5 years) is up for repaving. Propose a Vision-Zero + Complete-Streets + frequency-vs-coverage-informed redesign: lane configuration, bike + bus + pedestrian elements, speed-management tools, and how you'd respond to community objections about lost parking + lost vehicle capacity.

question.question: A BRT line averages 25 km/h with 90-second peak headways + 80 passengers per articulated bus per direction. What is the approximate peak capacity (passengers per hour per direction, PPHPD)?

question.prompt: In ≤140 words, explain why the 15-minute city (Moreno) + TOD (Calthorpe) + Jacobs's four conditions converge on a common urban form.
question.rubric: Mentions: All three frameworks identify the *same* spatial structure: dense, mixed-use, walkable, fine-grain blocks where daily needs (work, food, school, health, leisure) are reachable on foot, bike, or short transit ride. Jacobs (1961) — mixed primary uses + short blocks + varied building ages + sufficient density. Calthorpe TOD (1993) — compact mixed-use within 5-10 min walk of high-quality transit. Moreno's 15-minute city (2016) — every resident accesses six functions within 15-min walk or bike. They converge because the spatial logic is the same: proximity + diversity + density + walkability. Differences are emphasis (Jacobs micro-empirical, Calthorpe transit-anchored regional, Moreno accessibility-centered). Combined with Vision Zero (safe streets) + Shoup (no parking minimums) + Walker (frequent transit), they define the contemporary integrated transportation + land-use agenda.
